title: Grade 11 Physics — Gravitation
description: Newton's law of gravitation, g, Kepler's laws, orbital velocity, escape velocity, satellites (CBSE Ch. 8)
subject: physics

questions.question: Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation states that the gravitational force between two bodies is:
options: Directly proportional to the sum of their masses and inversely proportional to the distance between them
Directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them
Directly proportional to the product of their masses and directly proportional to the distance
Inversely proportional to the product of masses and inversely proportional to the square of distance
questions.explanation: F = Gm₁m₂/r². The force is proportional to the product of masses (m₁ × m₂) and inversely proportional to the square of the distance (r²) between their centres. G is the Universal Gravitational Constant.

questions.question: The value of the Universal Gravitational Constant G is approximately:
questions.explanation: G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². G is an extremely small constant — gravity is actually the weakest of the four fundamental forces. The value was first measured experimentally by Henry Cavendish in 1798.

questions.question: The acceleration due to gravity at Earth's surface (g) is related to Earth's mass M and radius R by:
questions.explanation: For a mass m at Earth's surface: Weight = mg = GMm/R². Dividing both sides by m: g = GM/R². This shows g depends on Earth's mass and radius, not on the falling object's mass.

questions.question: How does g (acceleration due to gravity) vary as you go above Earth's surface to height h?
options: g increases because you get closer to the Moon's gravity
g remains constant up to 100 km altitude
g decreases because r (distance from centre) increases — g ∝ 1/r²
questions.explanation: g = GM/(R + h)². As h increases, (R + h) increases, so g decreases. At height h << R: g_h ≈ g(1 − 2h/R). Beyond Earth's atmosphere, g continues to decrease following the inverse-square law.

questions.question: The acceleration due to gravity at Earth's centre is:
questions.explanation: At Earth's centre, the gravitational pull from all surrounding mass cancels out equally in all directions. Also, g at depth d = g(1 − d/R). At the centre, d = R, so g = 0. There is no net gravitational force at Earth's centre.

questions.question: A person weighs 60 N on Earth. Their approximate weight on the Moon would be:
questions.explanation: g_Moon ≈ g_Earth/6. Weight on Moon = 60/6 = 10 N. This is because the Moon has smaller mass and radius than Earth. Astronauts feel much lighter on the Moon — they can jump much higher!

questions.question: Escape velocity is the minimum speed needed to:
options: Put a satellite into circular orbit
Escape a body's gravitational field without further propulsion
Travel at the speed of light
questions.explanation: Escape velocity (v_e) is the minimum launch speed needed to escape a body's gravitational field completely without any further thrust. For Earth: v_e = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR) ≈ 11.2 km/s.

questions.question: The orbital speed of a satellite in circular orbit at radius r from Earth's centre is:
questions.explanation: For circular orbit, gravitational force provides centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r → v² = GM/r → v = √(GM/r). Note: escape velocity = √(2GM/r) = √2 × orbital velocity.

questions.question: Kepler's First Law of Planetary Motion states that:
options: Planets move in circular orbits around the Sun
All planets move with the same speed
Planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one of the two foci
The time period of all planets is the same
questions.explanation: Kepler's 1st Law (Law of Orbits): Each planet moves in an elliptical orbit with the Sun at one focus. This was a major discovery — earlier astronomers assumed circular orbits. The point closest to the Sun is the perihelion; farthest is the aphelion.

questions.question: Kepler's Second Law (Law of Areas) states that a planet sweeps equal areas in equal times. This implies that:
options: Planets move fastest when farthest from the Sun
Planets always move at constant speed
Planets move faster when closer to the Sun and slower when farther away
questions.explanation: Equal areas in equal time (angular momentum conservation). When a planet is nearer the Sun (perihelion), it moves faster to sweep the same area as when it is at aphelion. This is a consequence of the conservation of angular momentum.

questions.question: Kepler's Third Law states T² ∝ a³, where T is the orbital period and a is the semi-major axis. This means:
options: Planets farther from the Sun have shorter orbital periods
The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis
All planets have the same orbital period
The orbit size and period are unrelated
questions.explanation: Kepler's 3rd Law (Law of Periods): T²/a³ = constant (same for all planets orbiting the Sun). Planets farther from the Sun (larger a) take longer to complete one orbit — Earth takes 1 year, Jupiter takes ≈ 12 years.

questions.question: A geostationary satellite has a time period of approximately:
questions.explanation: A geostationary satellite orbits the Earth with a period of 24 hours (= Earth's rotation period). It stays above a fixed point on the equator — essential for communication satellites, weather satellites, and TV broadcasting.

questions.question: The gravitational potential energy (U) of a mass m at distance r from a body of mass M is:
questions.explanation: U = −GMm/r. The negative sign indicates that the gravitational force is attractive — energy must be supplied to separate the masses. U = 0 at r = ∞ (reference), and becomes more negative as r decreases.

questions.question: If the radius of the Earth were doubled with its mass unchanged, the acceleration due to gravity at the surface would:
questions.explanation: g = GM/R². If R doubles, g becomes GM/(2R)² = GM/4R² = g/4. So g reduces to one-fourth of its original value. This shows why gravity on large planets is very strong despite their greater radius — mass grows even faster.

questions.question: The escape velocity from Earth (≈ 11.2 km/s) is related to orbital velocity (≈ 7.9 km/s at the surface) by the factor:
questions.explanation: v_escape = √(2GM/R) = √2 × √(GM/R) = √2 × v_orbital. So escape velocity = √2 × orbital velocity ≈ 1.41 × 7.9 km/s ≈ 11.2 km/s. Escape velocity is always √2 times the circular orbital velocity at that radius.
